conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your doctors here. You were transferred to us because your feeding tube got clogged. Can you tell me if you're having any pain or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have pain here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Points to abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for letting me know. I see you're on a trach collar and not running a ventilator now. That's good progress from your recent pneumonia. Any fever, cough, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Breathing okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your sputum cultures showed Proteus and Pseudomonas, but you’ve already completed a 10-day course of Unasyn for that. No blood infection. You’re past the worst of the pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube not working. Can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why you’re here. Your GJ tube clogged, and the team at the other hospital couldn’t unclog it. You haven’t been getting your feeds or medicines through it since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medicines? Like my HIV pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve been missing your Truvada, darunavir, and other meds. We’ll fix that once we replace the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put in a new tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Interventional radiology is scheduled to replace it today. It’s a quick procedure under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation so you’ll be comfortable. They’ll use a wire to guide the new tube in. It usually goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure just finished. They successfully replaced your GJ tube with a new low-profile one. It’s ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition will start tube feeds slowly this afternoon. Once we confirm it’s working, we’ll restart your HIV meds and other oral medications through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your liver enzymes are a bit high—ALT and AST are elevated. We did an ultrasound, which showed gallstones, but no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gallstones? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The stones aren’t causing inflammation. The liver enzyme rise might be from your HIV meds or past infections. We’ll need your primary doctor to follow this up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. Just monitoring. We’ll make sure your PCP checks it in the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your feeds are going well. No leaks or discomfort. We’ve restarted your HIV medications—Truvada, darunavir, ritonavir—and your seizure medicine, levetiracetam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about missing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Staying on schedule with your HIV meds is important. Your viral load is undetectable, and your CD4 count is 168, so your treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the steroids I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were started on methylprednisolone because your morning cortisol was low—5.9. But since you’re stable and not in shock anymore, we’re stopping the steroids now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I felt jittery on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing remains stable on the trach collar. The chest X-ray shows your lungs are clear, though there are some chronic changes from past infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still need oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue needing oxygen through your trach at home. That hasn’t changed. But you’re off the ventilator and pressors, which is excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night well. Vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where am I going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To a skilled nursing facility—we’ll send the name. They can manage your trach, feeds, and medications, and help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I come back here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless needed. But you’ll follow up with your primary doctor soon, especially for the liver enzyme issue and gallstones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on levetiracetam twice daily. That hasn’t changed. As long as you keep taking it, your seizures should remain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You handled this really well. Keep up with your feeds, meds, and trach care. We’ll send all instructions to the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your new tube is intact, no redness. You’ve had regular bowel movements and no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeds feel normal. No pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll document everything for the nursing team. You’re cleared to transfer later this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. One last thing—your discharge summary says to use sodium bicarbonate if the tube clogs again, and keep using glycopyrrolate for secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. And call if you develop fever, belly pain, or trouble breathing. Otherwise, keep following up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. ___.
